title: Toukie Smith, ‘227’ Star and Ex‑De Niro Partner, Dies at 74 – Deadline Reports
body:
The entertainment world mourns the loss of Toukie Smith, the charismatic actress best known for her role as Eva Rawley on the beloved 1980s sitcom *227*. Smith passed away on November 4 at the age of 74, leaving behind a legacy that spanned television, film, and the high‑profile circles of Hollywood’s elite. Her death marks the end of a vibrant career that helped shape the representation of Black women on mainstream American television and cemented her as a memorable figure in pop culture history.

Born in New York City in 1950, Smith first entered the public eye as a model before transitioning to acting in the late 1970s. Her breakthrough came in 1985 when she joined the cast of *227* as the flamboyant, quick‑witted Eva Rawley, a character who quickly became a fan favorite for her sharp humor and unapologetic confidence. The show, which centered on the everyday lives of residents in a Washington, D.C., apartment building, provided a rare platform for a predominantly Black ensemble during a time when such representation was limited. Smith’s performance not only contributed to the series’ five‑season run but also helped pave the way for future sitcoms featuring strong Black female leads.

Beyond *227*, Smith demonstrated a versatile range that took her from the neon‑lit streets of *Miami Vice*—where she appeared in several episodes as a recurring guest—to the silver screen. Her film credits include supporting roles in *The Last Dragon* (1985) and *The Color of Money* (1986), where she shared the screen with cinematic heavyweights. Although she never achieved leading‑lady status in Hollywood’s blockbuster arena, her steady presence across mediums underscored a career built on resilience and adaptability. Colleagues often recalled her professionalism and warm demeanor on set, qualities that made her a respected figure among peers.

Smith’s personal life intersected with the film industry’s most iconic name when she entered a long‑term relationship with actor Robert De Niro in the early 1990s. The couple, who never married, welcomed twins—Airyn and Julian—in 1995. Their partnership, while occasionally spotlighted by tabloids, was largely kept private, reflecting Smith’s desire to protect her family from the relentless glare of celebrity scrutiny. In later years, she and De Niro amicably separated, yet both continued to co‑parent their children, maintaining a low‑key family dynamic that underscored Smith’s commitment to her role as a mother.

The news of Smith’s passing resonated deeply within the entertainment community, prompting an outpouring of tributes on social media and from former co‑stars. *227* creator Michael G. Michele praised her “unmatched energy and comedic timing,” while *Miami Vice* director Michael Mann highlighted her “ability to bring depth to even the smallest of roles.” Fans remembered her signature catchphrase, “Honey, you better believe it,” as a cultural touchstone that still echoes in reruns and streaming platforms. Her influence extends beyond nostalgia; contemporary actors cite Smith as an early inspiration for embracing bold, unapologetic characters that defy stereotypes.

As the industry reflects on her contributions, Smith’s legacy serves as a reminder of the progress made—and the work still required—to ensure diverse stories receive mainstream platforms. Her career trajectory illustrates how talent, when combined with perseverance, can break barriers and inspire future generations of performers. While her twins now navigate adulthood without their mother’s guiding presence, they inherit a narrative of strength and artistic dedication that will continue to inspire.

Looking ahead, the enduring popularity of *227* and the renewed interest in classic 1980s television suggest that Smith’s work will remain accessible to new audiences. Streaming services are poised to re‑introduce her performances to viewers worldwide, ensuring that Eva Rawley’s wit and charm endure. In honoring Toukie Smith, the entertainment world not only commemorates a beloved actress but also reaffirms its commitment to celebrating the diverse voices that have shaped its history.
